newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaireans defy protest ban, Tutsis flee.
newsitem.headline: Zaireans defy protest ban, Tutsis flee.

text.p: Zaireans blocked roads and hijacked cars in Kinshasa on Tuesday, defying a government ban on protests, and more Tutsis fled the capital.
More than 1,000 Tutsis are estimated to have left Kinshasa since an ethnic-Tutsi rebellion broke out in eastern Zaire two weeks ago overwhelming the Zaire army there.

Protests erupted in many parts of the sprawling city but the focus was the university campus in central Kinshasa. Despite a police cordon, students broke out to vent their anger over the government's handling of the fighting.
Students said one demonstrator was killed. "He was shot by an army colonel when he was trying to steal a car," one of the students said.
No official confirmation was available for the report.
Students cruised the city in dozens of stolen vehicles, calling for part-Tutsi Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo to go and radical opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi to take his place.
"Tshisekedi come back quickly, Kengo has sold the country," they chanted. Tshisekedi was prime minister briefly before being sacked by President Mobutu Sese Seseko in 1993.

Security forces with riot shields did not stop the protests until they reached the imposing People's Parliament, home of Zaire's transition parliament, where a line of troops prevented marchers from advancing.
Most businesses closed by 3 p.m. and commuters were stranded as taxi and bus drivers left the streets in fear.
Earlier about 300 to 500 demonstrated in a city avenue.
"They threw stones at the car and tried to steal it. I just drove very fast," said a taxi driver in central Kinshasa.
Zaire on Monday banned demonstrations and authorised troops to open fire on anyone caught looting or engaging in vandalism.

A statement issued after a special cabinet meeting said the measures had become necessary because of attacks on Rwandans and Burundians in Zaire following a Tutsi revolt in the east. Zaire accuses Rwandan troops of fighting alongside the rebels.
Protesters, notably students, view the ban as intended to protect Kengo who is accused of being soft on the rebellion.
"We will increase pressure until Kengo leaves. A Rwandan Prime Minister cannot fight a war against Rwanda," said student activist Pierre Wadi.
Hundreds of Tutsis hounded in anger after Tutsi rebels wrested control of much of Zaire's two eastern provinces were trying to flee the capital, witnesses said.
A boat with 70 Tutsis arrived at Brazzaville, capital of neighbouring Congo just across the river Zaire from Kinshasa.

"On the boat some Zaireans said they would throw us into the water and kill us, but other Zaireans prevented them from doing so," A Tutsi woman passenger, who asked not to be named, said by telephone.
Onlookers jeered and threatened another 65 Tutsi men, women and children who waited to cross the river.
"If I was in charge I would pour petrol on them and burn the lot," said one of the soldiers protecting the Tutsis.
"In Rwanda and Burundi they would not let Zaireans leave so easily as we have," said a Zairean port official.
The military shielded the Tutsis until they crossed.
Some Tutsis said they paid up to $3,000 a head to cross in dugout canoes. About 400 crossed in such canoes on Monday.
Many more Tutsis are still hiding in safe houses in Kinshasa, waiting for an opportunity to leave.
Relatives and friends are still looking for missing Tutsis who have disappeared after their houses were looted and destroyed in the recent disturbances.
